newsitem.title: USA: Insurers hope court eases Superfund cleanup costs.
newsitem.headline: Insurers hope court eases Superfund cleanup costs.

text.p: U.S. insurance groups turned to a federal appeals court on Friday to help relieve them from covering cleanup costs at old hazardous waste dumps.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit in Atlanta heard arguments on Friday in a closely-watched case in which the government challenged a lower court ruling that Olin Corp should not be held liable for cleaning a site where it dumped waste before the Superfund law was enacted in 1980.
If the appeals court upholds the decision, the government would have to pay billions of dollars for environmental cleanup that companies now pay.
"The case has potential for massive consequences if the company's argument prevails," said John Hanson, a partner at the law firm Beveridge and Diamond.

In a surprise move earlier this year, a lower court judge backed the chemicals producer, saying Congress had not intended Superfund liability to apply retroactively and the law overreached the government's ability to mandate activities within a state.
Assistant attorney general Lois Schiffer on Friday asked the appeals court to rule quickly on the case because it had spawned a number of cases that have stalled cleanup work.
"I think this case is a creating fair amount of disruption in our ability to move forward with Superfund cleanups," Schiffer told Reuters.

Connecticut-based Olin Corp, supported by insurance firms, argued that a 1994 Supreme Court ruling, dubbed Landgraf, established that, if a law was to apply retroactively, Congress had to expressly provide for it in the language of the law, or make it clear in debate leading up to the passage of the law. The Clinton administration's appeal hinged on the argument that the 1980 Superfund law was retroactive because it was designed to tackle toxic dumps like Love Canal.
Schiffer argued that every single court, except in this case, had backed retroactive liability and the government's ability regulate hazardous wastes.

But oil and chemical companies, who are responsible for the bulk of toxic waste cleanup costs both directly and through taxes that fund the Superfund trust fund, were not counting on the courts to relieve them.
"Our strategy has always been to seek necessary changes to the law through the legislative process," said Owen Kean, a spokesman for the Chemical Manufacturers Association.

While opposed to retroactive liability, oil and chemical companies fear that if the government is made totally responsible for all pre-1980 cleanup costs, Washington might raise taxes further on their industries to pay for it.
Observers expect the appeals court to rule by spring 1997, and expect an appeal to the Supreme Court.
